items.title: Decline is not the end — vinyl records came back
items.claim: Vinyl record sales collapsed from the mid-1980s as CDs took over. What has happened since the late 2000s?

options.text: Vinyl sales have risen every year from 2007 to 2023, overtaking CDs in US revenue terms in 2022 for the first time since 1987 (RIAA data)

items.reveal:
RIAA US data: vinyl revenue fell to under $20m by 2006. By 2022, vinyl revenue was $1.2bn — overtaking CDs ($483m) for the first time in 35 years. UK Official Charts data shows similar pattern from 2008 onwards.

The textbook PLC implies decline is terminal. Brand repositioning, nostalgia and physical-product premiums in a streaming world reversed that trajectory. Other examples: Polaroid film, Kodak Super 8, mechanical watches.
items.why: The four-stage product life cycle is a framework, not a law of nature. Decline can be reversed by changing what the product means to customers.

items.title: Just-in-time becomes a vulnerability under shock
items.claim: Toyota pioneered just-in-time inventory. What happened to Toyota production during the 2011 Tohoku earthquake?

options.text: Toyota's global production fell by around 800,000 vehicles because a single supplier of microcontrollers (Renesas) was damaged

items.reveal:
Renesas's Naka factory in Ibaraki produced ~30% of automotive microcontrollers globally. After the 11 March 2011 earthquake, Toyota's worldwide output dropped sharply through to mid-2011. After Tohoku, Toyota mandated suppliers to map upstream dependencies and hold buffer stocks for critical components — partially abandoning pure JIT.

The 2020-22 COVID semiconductor shortages repeated the lesson industry-wide.
items.why: Lean optimises against ordinary variation. It does not optimise against catastrophic disruption — and the same firms that pioneered it have had to add 'just-in-case' buffers.

items.title: Brand value can exceed half of market capitalisation
items.claim: Interbrand's 2023 Best Global Brands ranking valued Apple's brand at around $502 billion. What's the relationship between brand value and accounting?

options.text: Brand value appears directly on the balance sheet for all firms
Under IFRS / UK GAAP, internally generated brands are not recognised as balance sheet assets; purchased brands can be. Apple's $502bn estimate is an external valuation, not a reported figure
Brand value equals market cap minus debt
Brand value has no relationship with share price

items.reveal:
IAS 38 prohibits capitalising internally generated brands; accounting wants to avoid the manipulability of self-assessed intangibles. Acquired brands (e.g. Cadbury bought by Kraft for £11.5bn in 2010) appear at acquisition cost as 'goodwill' or identified intangibles.

Interbrand, Kantar BrandZ and Brand Finance use different methodologies — discounted cash flow from brand-attributable earnings — and produce different rankings. The numbers are estimates, but the underlying point is real: a meaningful share of S&P 500 market value sits in intangibles invisible on balance sheets.
items.why: Investors price intangibles even when accountants don't book them. The gap between book and market value for brand-heavy firms is largely brand and goodwill.
